A needle with three separate eye holes along its shaft
A 'Leather' (wedge / cutting point) needle with sharp chisel edges that slice through dense hides
A super-fine ballpoint silk needle
7.explanation: Wedge-shaped cutting points pierce clean knife slits through tough leather grains, preventing needle deflection and skipped stitches.

7.question: What do the numbers on sewing machine needle sizing mean (e.g. 70/10 vs 100/16)?
options: The price of the needle in local currency coins
The number of stitches the needle can sew per second
The maximum length of thread that can fit through the needle eye
The diameter/thickness of the needle blade (the first is metric in hundredths of a mm, the second is American sizing; higher = thicker)
7.explanation: Size 70/10 measures 0.70 mm blade thickness (fine silks); size 100/16 measures 1.00 mm blade thickness (heavy denim, canvas).

7.question: What is the primary function of an 'Overlocker' (Serger) sewing machine?
options: To sew buttonholes on tailored business suit jackets
To embroider complex multi-coloured floral designs on silk
To press finished garments with hot pressurized steam
To trim fabric raw edges with built-in knives and encase the edge with multi-thread loopers in a single high-speed operation
7.explanation: Simultaneous edge trimming and chain-loop overcasting (3, 4, or 5 threads) produces professional, stretch-compatible seams on knits and wovens.

7.question: How does an overlocker stitch accommodate stretchy knit fabrics better than a standard lockstitch?
options: Overlockers use elastic rubber wire instead of normal thread
Overlockers melt the edges of the fabric together with heat
Overlock stitches are formed of interlocking thread loops that stretch and expand naturally with the fabric without snapping
Overlockers glue the seam together with liquid rubber cement
7.explanation: Interlooping upper and lower looper threads flex dynamically in accordion-like waveforms, accommodating high knit elasticity without thread breakage.

7.question: What is 'differential feed' on an overlocker machine?
options: Two separate feed dogs moving at different relative speeds to prevent stretchy knits from waving (stretching) or puckering during sewing
Feeding two different colours of thread into the same needle
A motor that runs at two different electrical voltages
A pedal that changes the speed of the cutting knives
7.explanation: Adjusting the front feed dog speed relative to the rear allows sewists to stretch or gather fabric, eliminating wavy lettuce edges on knits.

7.question: What is a 'zipper foot' on a sewing machine?
options: A narrow presser foot that attaches on either the left or right side, allowing stitching extremely close to zipper teeth without riding over them
A foot that zips open when you step on the foot pedal
A foot made of sharp metal zipper teeth that cuts fabric
A foot used exclusively to sew winter hiking boots
7.explanation: Asymmetrical narrow single-toe geometry allows close needle access adjacent to raised plastic or metal coiled zipper elements.

7.question: What is an 'invisible zipper foot'?
options: A specialized presser foot with parallel grooves on the underside that unroll and flatten concealed zipper coils while stitching directly beneath them
A foot that cannot be seen by the human eye
A presser foot made of completely clear transparent glass
A foot that sews zippers without using any sewing thread
7.explanation: Parallel grooved soles mechanically unroll inward-coiled nylon zipper spirals, placing the stitch line tight against the coil for invisible seams.

7.question: What is a 'buttonhole foot' (automatic 1-step or 4-step foot)?
options: A presser foot that holds a button to measure its length, automatically stitching a precision balanced bar-tacked buttonhole to fit it
A foot that cuts round holes through fabric with razor blades
A foot used to sew shoe soles onto running sneakers
A foot that glues buttons onto shirts with hot melted plastic
7.explanation: Sliding gauge frames read button diameters, coordinating needle swing and reverse feeding to stitch dense satin-stitch side beads and end bar-tacks.

7.question: What is a 'walking foot' (even feed foot)?
options: A foot used to sew leather shoes while walking outdoors
A foot that counts how many steps a tailor walks in a day
An attachment with its own upper feed teeth that move synchronized with the lower feed dogs, feeding slippery, bulky, or quilted layers evenly
A mechanical foot that walks across the table by itself
7.explanation: Driven by the needle clamp arm, upper vibrating feed dogs grip slick or thick multi-layer sandwiches (quilts, velvet), preventing layer slippage.

7.question: What is a 'seam ripper' (stitch unpicker)?
options: A metal clamp used to hold fabric rolls onto tables
A heavy pair of shears used to cut thick denim fabric
A small handheld tool with a sharp curved blade and fine point used to cut and remove unwanted or mistaken stitches safely
A pointed screwdriver used to repair sewing machine motors
7.explanation: The fine point slips beneath individual thread stitches while the protected ball prevents the curved razor blade from slicing fashion cloth.

7.question: What is a 'tailor's ham' used for in garment pressing?
options: A wooden mallet used to hammer metal grommets into belts
A firm, ham-shaped curved pressing cushion used to press and shape three-dimensional curved seams (darts, bust curves, sleeve heads)
A smoked meat sandwich eaten by tailors during lunch breaks
A heavy iron weight used to hold fabric flat during cutting
7.explanation: Sawdust-stuffed curved profiles (wool on one side, cotton on the other) allow steam to mold and set darts without creasing surrounding cloth.

7.question: What is a 'sleeve board' used for in pressing?
options: A wooden paddle used to beat wool coats clean in rivers
A board used to carry finished shirts across factory floors
A flat ruler used to draw sleeve pattern lines on paper
A small, narrow, padded two-level ironing board designed to press narrow cylindrical sleeve and trouser seams without creasing the opposite side
7.explanation: Elevated narrow cantilever arms allow tubular sleeves to slide on cleanly, pressing underarm seams without imprinting front creases.

7.question: What is a 'seam roll'?
options: A roll of sticky adhesive tape used to remove pet hair
A freshly baked bread roll served in tailoring cafeterias
A roll of paper towels used to clean oil spills in factories
A cylindrical, sausage-shaped padded cushion used for pressing long, narrow seams (such as sleeve or pant seams) open without edge pressing marks
7.explanation: Convex cylindrical curvature raises the seam ridge above the board, preventing iron heat from pressing seam allowance edges through to the face.

7.question: What is a 'tailor's clapper' made of hardwood used for?
options: A wooden board used to chop vegetables in fashion cafeterias
A heavy wooden hammer used to drive nails into tailoring tables
A smooth, unvarnished wooden block pressed firmly onto freshly steamed wool seams to absorb steam, trap heat, and set razor-sharp, flat edges
A wooden musical instrument played in fashion studio parties
7.explanation: Dense unvarnished hardwood (beech, maple) rapidly wicks moisture and traps steam heat within wool fibres, freezing flat, sharp tailored edges.

7.question: What is the difference between 'pressing' and 'ironing' in professional garment making?
options: Pressing is done with a rolling pin; ironing uses a hair dryer
Pressing is lifting and lowering the iron vertically with steam in specific spots; ironing is sliding the iron back and forth across fabric
Pressing is done by dry cleaners; ironing is done by teenagers
Pressing is done with cold water; ironing is done with hot fire
7.explanation: Sliding irons across wet seams stretches bias edges out of shape; up-and-down vertical pressing preserves fabric geometry and molds volume.

7.question: Why should sewing machine bobbin cases and feed dogs be cleaned regularly of lint and dust?
options: Lint makes the machine light bulb change colour to blue
Lint makes the sewing machine run at three times its normal speed
Accumulated lint absorbs machine oil, jams mechanism rotation, causes skipped stitches, and creates thread tension problems
Lint turns into poisonous chemical gas if left inside the machine
7.explanation: Fluff compacted between feed dog teeth and race hooks causes friction, increases motor load, and alters delicate tension calibrations.

7.question: What type of lubricant should be applied to sewing machine metal moving parts?
options: Liquid honey or sweet pancake syrup
Vegetable cooking oil or olive oil from the kitchen
Specially formulated, clear, non-gumming mineral sewing machine oil
Heavy black automotive motor engine oil
7.explanation: Low-viscosity, non-gumming refined mineral oils lubricate high-speed mechanical bearings without polymerizing or staining textiles.

7.question: What is a 'rotary cutter' used with a self-healing cutting mat and acrylic ruler?
options: A tool used to punch decorative holes in leather belts
A handheld magnifying glass used to inspect fabric threads
A motorized circular saw used to cut through tree trunks
A circular pizza-wheel-like blade tool that rolls smoothly to cut multiple fabric plies with high precision and speed
7.explanation: Rolling tungsten carbide circular blades slice clean straight edges along rigid acrylic rulers without shifting underlying fabric plies.

7.question: What is an 'embroidery hoop' used for in hand embroidery?
options: A plastic hula-hoop used for exercising during morning work breaks
A decorative circular picture frame hung on a living room wall
A circular magnifying glass held above a sewing machine
A pair of concentric wooden or plastic rings that clamp fabric taut like a drum to keep stitches smooth, even, and unpuckered
7.explanation: Tensioned drum-like clamping maintains uniform thread tension and prevents needle stitch shrinkage from puckering ground fabrics.

7.question: What is a 'bodkin' used for in garment sewing?
options: A blunt, heavy needle-like tool or tweezer used to thread elastic, tape, or cording through an enclosed waistband or hem casing
A pointed needle used to sew buttons onto suit cuffs
A sharp carving knife used to cut wooden tailoring blocks
A heavy iron tool used to bend metal sewing machine arms
7.explanation: Smooth ball tips and secure grip teeth glide freely through narrow fabric tunnels without catching, poking, or piercing casing walls.

7.question: What is a 'thimble' and why is it worn on the middle finger during hand sewing?
options: A metal whistle blown by tailors to signal lunch breaks
A small pitted metal or leather cap that protects the fingertip and provides a firm surface to push the needle through dense fabric
A piece of silver jewellery worn on fashion runway shows
A small metal cup used to drink water while working
7.explanation: Small indentations on the thimble crown capture needle eyes, allowing the strong middle finger to exert forward force without painful punctures.

7.question: What is a 'needle threader'?
options: A special sewing needle that has no eye hole at all
A machine that automatically winds spools of cotton thread
A pair of glasses worn by tailors to read small instruction text
A small tool with a fine flexible diamond-shaped wire loop used to draw thread easily through the small eye of a hand or machine needle
7.explanation: Collapsible fine steel wire passes through minuscule needle eyes, capturing thread and pulling it back through effortlessly.

7.question: What are 'dressmaker's pins' (dress pins)?
options: Fine, sharp steel pins with small metal or glass heads used to hold fabric layers together temporarily during cutting and sewing
Small metal safety pins used to pin price tags to garments
Heavy iron nails used to build wooden tailor tables
Large decorative hairpins worn by fashion models on runways
7.explanation: Smooth, nickel-plated steel pins pierce fine textile weaves without snagging filaments, holding seams temporarily prior to basting.

7.question: Why are 'glass-headed pins' preferred over plastic-headed pins when sewing?
options: Glass-headed pins can be eaten as a nutritious snack
Glass-headed pins are three times lighter than air
The glass heads will not melt if accidentally touched by a hot household pressing iron
Glass-headed pins turn bright red when fabric is sewn properly
7.explanation: High thermal resistance prevents catastrophic plastic melt stains from adhering to the soleplate and ruining fashion fabrics.

7.question: What is a 'loop turner'?
options: A motorized turntable used to display shoes in shop windows
A round wooden brush used to comb wool coats clean
A pair of pliers used to pull bent needles out of machines
A long, slender wire tool with a tiny latch-hook at one end used to turn narrow fabric spaghetti straps or rouleau loops right side out
7.explanation: Latching onto the internal end of a sewn fabric tube allows it to be pulled smoothly back through its own hollow channel.

7.question: What is a 'point turner' (collar point turner)?
options: A pair of tweezers used to pluck loose threads from seams
A motorized drill used to make buttonholes in leather belts
A sharp pencil used to draw sketches on fashion mood boards
A smooth, pointed plastic or wooden handheld tool used to push out sharp corners on collars, cuffs, and lapels without poking holes
7.explanation: Blunt tapered points push turned collar points into crisp, square corners from within without puncturing fragile seam junctions.

7.question: What is an 'industrial bar-tack machine' used for in commercial apparel manufacturing?
options: A machine that irons pants using high-pressure steam rollers
A machine that serves cold sodas to factory workers during breaks
A specialized sewing machine that sews a dense, short repeated zigzag stitch to reinforce high-stress points (pocket corners, belt loops, fly bases)
A machine that cuts wooden shipping pallets into small firewood sticks
7.explanation: High-speed automated bar-tack cycles deposit high-density perpendicular stitches, distributing localized shear strain on pocket edges.

7.question: What is a 'blind-hem machine' (or blind-stitch machine)?
options: A machine operated exclusively in completely dark rooms
A machine that cuts fabric without measuring with rulers
A specialized sewing machine that uses a curved needle to catch only a single yarn of the outer fabric, creating an invisible hem on the face
A machine that sews seams with eyes closed for blind workers
7.explanation: Horizontal benders flex hem folds so the oscillating curved needle penetrates only half the face yarn depth, leaving zero face stitch marks.

7.question: What is a 'twin needle' (double needle) on a domestic sewing machine?
options: A pair of sewing needles tied together with rubber bands
Two needles mounted on a single crossbar from one shank, producing two parallel rows of straight stitching on the face and a zigzag on the reverse
A needle with two eyes drilled into the same single shaft
Two separate sewing machines operating side by side on a table
7.explanation: Twin needles thread two spools into a single bobbin zigzag, creating flexible, professional-looking twin-needle hems on t-shirts and activewear.

7.question: What is a 'button-sewing foot'?
options: A foot used to iron button plackets flat after washing
A machine that manufactures plastic buttons from melted resin
A foot that sews zippers into trousers automatically
A small, rubber-cushioned foot that grips flat buttons firmly against the fabric while the machine zigzags across the button holes
7.explanation: Rubberized prongs immobilize 2-hole or 4-hole buttons over drop-feed dogs while zero-length zigzag stitches anchor shank-less buttons rapidly.

7.question: Why must the feed dogs be DROPPED or covered with a darning plate when sewing on buttons with a machine?
options: So the machine does not try to move the fabric forward while stitching in place through the stationary button holes
To prevent the button from changing colour during sewing
To turn on the machine internal light bulb automatically
To make the sewing machine needle move twice as fast
7.explanation: Disengaging feed transport confines needle penetration to stationary lateral zigzag swings, preventing needle collisions with plastic button rims.

7.question: What is 'back-stitching' (reversing) at the beginning and end of a machine-sewn seam?
options: Sewing with the reverse side of the fabric facing upward
Stitching backward for 3–4 stitches over the initial stitches to securely lock the thread ends and prevent the seam from unraveling
Taking out stitches with a seam ripper because of an error
Sewing an entire garment in reverse while walking backwards
7.explanation: Reverse stitch overlap anchors the lockstitch knot within fabric friction, preventing seam opening under mechanical tensile stress.

7.question: What is 'basting' (tacking) in garment construction?
options: Temporary long, loose hand or machine stitches used to hold fabric layers in place for fitting or stitching, removed after final sewing
Gluing fabric pieces together with hot chemical spray glue
Pouring melted butter over roast meat during kitchen cooking
Sewing permanent heavy nylon stitches along a jacket hem
7.explanation: Long running stitches temporarily hold complex collars, sleeves, or zippers, allowing try-on adjustments before permanent lockstitching.

7.question: What is 'stay-stitching'?
options: Stitching an ironed garment to a wooden hanger so it stays neat
Sewing a seam three times with heavy carpet thread
Stitching a label inside a coat that says 'Stay Clean'
A row of permanent straight machine stitching sewn within the seam allowance on curved or bias edges (like necklines) to prevent stretching during handling
7.explanation: Placed 3 mm inside the seam allowance, stay-stitching stabilizes curved bias grain yarns before facings or collars are attached.

7.question: What is 'understitching' on a facing or collar?
options: Stitching a secret hidden pocket on the inside of a coat
Stitching the seam allowances firmly to the facing close to the seamline, preventing the facing from rolling out and showing on the garment face
Sewing thermal winter underwear inside a pair of trousers
Sewing stitches underneath a sewing table on the floor
7.explanation: Catching the trimmed seam allowance to the facing prevents the internal lining from rolling over the knife-edge seam to the fashion exterior.

7.question: What is 'topstitching'?
options: A line of decorative or functional machine stitching sewn on the OUTSIDE (face) of a garment, parallel to a seam or edge (e.g. on jeans pockets)
Stitching sewn on the inside pocket lining of a jacket
Stitching done by the most senior, experienced tailor in a studio
Stitching sewn on the top roof of a clothing factory
7.explanation: Sewn with heavy topstitching thread and longer stitch lengths (3–4 mm), topstitching accents design lines and anchors internal facings flat.

7.question: What is 'edge-stitching'?
options: Cutting the edge of a fabric with pinking shears
Painting the edge of a garment with fluorescent fabric paint
Sewing around the edge of a room on the baseboard wood
A line of topstitching sewn extremely close (approx. 1–2 mm) to a finished folded edge or seamline for a clean, tailored finish
7.explanation: Stitched a millimeter from the creased fold, edge-stitching crisply secures collars, pocket hems, and front shirt bands.

7.question: What is 'grading' (layering) a seam allowance?
options: Trimming the individual layers of a seam allowance to different widths (e.g. widest layer to the outside) to reduce bulk and prevent ridge marks
Measuring the width of a fabric roll with a wooden ruler
Sorting sewing needles by size into small plastic boxes
Grading student sewing tests in a fashion school class
7.explanation: Stepping enclosed seam layers (e.g. 6 mm, 9 mm, 12 mm) feathers internal thickness, eliminating unsightly external press ridges.

7.question: What is 'clipping' a curved seam allowance?
options: Attaching plastic laundry clips to clothes on a clothesline
Trimming loose threads from garment seams with scissors
Cutting off all buttons from a winter overcoat with pliers
Making small inward snips into the seam allowance on an inside (concave) curve (like a neckline) so the allowance can spread and lie flat when turned
7.explanation: Radial snips allow inward-turning seam allowances to spread open without buckling or puckering along concave curved collars and necklines.

7.question: What is 'notching' an outside (convex) curved seam allowance?
options: Sewing decorative notches along the bottom hem of a dress
Carving notches into the wooden legs of a sewing table
Cutting small V-shaped wedges out of the seam allowance on an outward curve (like a rounded collar corner) so it can contract without bunching
Poking holes through fabric with an electric drill
7.explanation: Excising small triangular wedges eliminates excess fabric mass, allowing outward convex edges to turn inside out crisp, flat, and un-bulked.

7.question: Why should pins NEVER be sewn over with a sewing machine needle?
options: The sewing machine motor will catch fire immediately
The thread will turn into solid steel wire
The needle can strike the pin, causing the needle to bend, shatter, break, damage the machine's timing, or fly into the sewer's eye
The pin will melt and turn the fabric bright green
7.explanation: High-velocity needle strikes on tempered steel pins chip needle points, burr hook races, throw needle-bar timing out, and pose eye injury hazards.

7.question: What safety precaution should always be taken before changing a sewing machine needle or presser foot?
options: Turn off all room lights in the tailoring workshop
Turn off the electrical power switch (or unplug the machine) to prevent accidental motor activation if the foot pedal is pressed
Put on heavy winter gloves and a warm woollen hat
Empty the water out of all household steam irons
7.explanation: Isolating electrical supply prevents accidental foot-pedal depression, guarding fingers against catastrophic motorized needle puncture injuries.

8.question: What is a 'plain seam' (flat seam)?
options: The most basic and common seam, made by placing two fabric pieces right sides together and stitching 1.5 cm from the raw edge, then pressing open
A seam glued together with chemical plastic adhesive
A seam sewn with five parallel rows of zig-zag stitching
A seam sewn with bright red embroidery thread on the face
8.explanation: The universal construction seam: joined face-to-face with a standard 1.5 cm allowance, pressed open or to one side, requiring edge neatening.

8.question: What is a 'French seam' and on what fabrics is it traditionally used?
options: A self-enclosing, narrow seam sewn twice (first wrong sides together, then right sides together) enclosing raw edges; used on sheer, lightweight fabrics
A heavy seam sewn with copper rivets on denim work jeans
A seam used exclusively to sew French military uniforms
A glued seam used on waterproof plastic raincoats
8.explanation: Enclosing raw edges completely within a 5 mm seam fold, French seams provide clean, elegant, fray-free transparency on chiffon and organza.

8.question: Why is a French seam UNSUITABLE for heavy, bulky fabrics like denim or winter wool?
options: French seams turn dark fabrics into bright white cloth
Sewing four layers of bulky fabric within a narrow enclosed seam creates an excessively thick, stiff, and uncomfortable ridge that cannot be pressed flat
French seams will dissolve in laundry washing machines if sewn on wool
French seams cause heavy fabrics to catch fire when pressed
8.explanation: Multi-ply fold bulk creates thick, unpressable ridges that chafe skin and distort external garment drape on medium-to-heavy textiles.

8.question: What is a 'flat-felled seam' (run-and-fell seam)?
options: An extremely strong, flat, durable seam where one seam allowance is trimmed and the other is folded over and stitched down flat (e.g. on jeans)
A seam used exclusively on silk evening wedding gowns
A seam that falls apart as soon as you touch it
A seam sewn with invisible transparent fishing line
8.explanation: Double topstitched flat-felled seams encase raw margins completely, offering superior tensile shear strength and flat abrasion resistance on jeans.

8.question: Why are flat-felled seams universally chosen for jeans and heavy workwear?
options: They take less than two seconds to sew on a sewing machine
They are exceptionally strong, completely encase raw edges, withstand frequent heavy industrial laundering, and resist tearing under strain
They require zero sewing thread to hold the fabric together
They make jeans completely waterproof like plastic bags
8.explanation: Interlocked folded construction and twin parallel stitch rows distribute tensile stress across heavy denim, preventing blowout under athletic strain.

8.question: What is an 'overcast seam' (serged seam)?
options: A seam sewn with cloudy grey thread on a rainy day
A seam sewn on the outside of a raincoat using clear glue
A seam that has been accidentally sewn in the wrong direction
A plain seam whose raw seam allowances are trimmed and encased together or separately with multi-thread overlock looper stitches
8.explanation: High-speed 3-thread or 4-thread overcasting binds raw edge threads cleanly, accommodating fabric flexibility and preventing fraying.

8.question: What is a 'bound seam' (Hong Kong finish)?
options: A couture seam finish where individual raw seam allowances are encased in narrow bias binding strips (often lightweight silk or rayon)
Tying two pieces of fabric together with thick jute rope
Burning the edges of fabric with a lighter to melt them
Gluing fabric edges together with plastic packaging tape
8.explanation: Hong Kong binding encases raw allowances in bias silk without bulk, delivering immaculate unlined jacket and luxury interior aesthetics.

8.question: What is a 'dart' in garment construction?
options: A tapered, wedge-shaped fold of fabric stitched on the wrong side to shape flat two-dimensional fabric to the three-dimensional curves of the body
A decorative button sewn onto the chest pocket of a shirt
A small hole punched through fabric with tailoring shears
A sharp pointed metal arrow thrown at a wooden dartboard
8.explanation: Darts fold out excess planar fabric wedge volume, transferring fullness smoothly over anatomical mounds (bust, shoulder blades, hips).

8.question: What is the 'apex' of a dart?
options: The wide open base of the dart located on the seamline
The sharp pointed tip of the dart where stitching tapers to an end, positioned pointing toward the fullest point of the body curve
The center line folded down the middle of the dart
The sewing machine needle used to stitch the dart
8.explanation: Stitching must feather cleanly off the fabric edge at the apex to prevent unsightly puckering or pointed 'dimples' over body mounds.

8.question: Why should darts be stitched from the wide end (seamline) toward the pointed tip (apex)?
options: Because the wide end of the dart is impossible to see
Stitching from the point makes the fabric catch fire
Tapering smoothly off the fabric fold at the point creates a smooth, rounded transition without puckers, dimples, or thread bunching
Stitching toward the point makes the sewing machine run faster
8.explanation: Directional stitching from base to apex allows sewing tension to diminish naturally, feathering off the folded edge in a gradual curve.

8.question: Why should the thread ends at a dart point NOT be back-stitched with the machine?
options: Back-stitching makes the sewing machine motor catch fire
Back-stitching causes the fabric to unravel instantly
Back-stitching makes the clothes iron melt during pressing
Back-stitching creates a thick, unsightly knot or dimple on the garment face; instead, sew off the fold and tie thread ends by hand
8.explanation: Machine reversing at the fragile apex creates concentrated thread knots that pull fabric into puckered dimples upon face pressing.

8.question: Which direction should vertical waist and contour darts be pressed?
options: Pressed open flat down the middle with scissors
Toward the outer side seams of the garment
Pressed upside down toward the shoulder seams
Toward the centre front or centre back of the garment
8.explanation: Standard tailoring conventions press vertical dart folds inward toward the central vertical axis to maintain anatomical symmetry.

8.question: Which direction should horizontal bust darts be pressed?
options: Folded backwards and cut off with scissors
Pressed open into a flat circle
Downward toward the bottom hem of the garment
Upward toward the shoulder seams
8.explanation: Pressing bust dart bulk downward prevents upward shadow lines and prevents downward-draping fabric folds from catching on the internal seam ridge.

8.question: What is a 'fish-tail dart' (double-pointed / contour dart)?
options: A dart cut in the shape of a live swimming fish
A decorative embroidery stitch used to hem tablecloths
A dart sewn onto the back of a marine diving suit
A vertical dart with two pointed ends that tapers in both directions from the middle, used to fit dresses and coats at the waist without a waist seam
8.explanation: Shaped like a diamond with dual apexes, it cinches excess fullness at the hollow waist while releasing ease across bust and hip mounds.

8.question: Why must a double-pointed fish-tail dart be clipped at the waistline before pressing?
options: To make a hole so a belt can pass through the dress
To allow air to cool the sewing machine needle
To remove half of the sewing stitches from the seam
To relieve fabric tension at the narrowest waist point, allowing the dart allowances to spread and lie flat against the curved body
8.explanation: Inward snips at the maximum waist suppression point relieve longitudinal tension, allowing dart folds to press flat without horizontal pulling.

8.question: What is 'gathers' in garment construction?
options: Folding fabric into crisp, sharp, permanent pleats with an iron
Collecting fallen pine cones from a forest floor
Drawing up fabric along parallel rows of loose running stitches to pull a wider piece of fabric into a smaller, controlled space (e.g. at cuffs or yokes)
Cutting fabric into tiny strips using electric rotary cutters
8.explanation: Pulling bobbin threads across two parallel gathering rows bunches soft, fluid ripples of fullness evenly into a fitted band or yoke.

8.question: How many rows of machine basting stitches should ideally be sewn to gather fabric evenly?
options: Only one single tight stitch in the center
No stitches; gathers are formed by gluing fabric with spray adhesive
Two (or three) parallel rows of long basting stitches, spaced 6 mm apart, with long thread tails left at both ends for pulling
Ten overlapping rows sewn with heavy carpet thread
8.explanation: Dual basting rows guide folds into uniform, vertical wavelets, preventing uneven bunching and protecting against thread breakage during pulling.

8.question: What are 'tucks' in garment design?
options: Loose threads hanging from the bottom hem of a jacket
Small plastic tags pinned to the collar of a shirt
Stitched folds of fabric sewn across part or all of their length on the garment face, providing both decorative texture and controlled fullness
Hidden pockets sewn inside the waistband of a pair of pants
8.explanation: Precision parallel vertical folds (pin-tucks, blind tucks, spaced tucks) add structural linear relief to Victorian blouses and tuxedo bibs.

8.question: What is a 'pin-tuck'?
options: A hole poked through fabric with dressmaking pins
A very narrow, delicate tuck (only 1–2 mm wide) stitched close to the fold, commonly used on fine vintage blouses, baby clothes, and shirts
A tuck held in place with metal safety pins instead of thread
A tuck sewn into heavy quilted winter ski jackets
8.explanation: Fine, hairline edge-stitched tucks create refined linear texture and subtle waist shaping on batiste, lawn, and silk chiffon.

8.question: What is a 'pleat'?
options: A fold formed by doubling fabric back upon itself and securing it at the top, allowing the fabric below to open and expand for movement and style
A piece of clear plastic tape stuck onto an ironed collar
A circle of fabric cut out with tailoring scissors
A tear ripped into the knee of a pair of denim pants
8.explanation: Engineered vertical folds (knife, box, inverted, accordion) introduce controlled dynamic expansion and volumetric drape to skirts.

8.question: What is an 'accordion pleat' (sunburst pleat)?
options: A flat seam sewn with heavy industrial copper rivets
A series of permanent, narrow, uniform pleats that fan out and expand like the bellows of an accordion, often heat-set into synthetic fabrics
A pleat that has been accidentally crushed in a washing machine
A musical instrument played by tailors in clothing factories
8.explanation: Heat-set into thermoplastic polyester fabrics, accordion pleating expands dramatically with bodily kinetic motion before snapping back.

8.question: What is a 'waistband' on skirts and trousers?
options: A fitted, reinforced band of fabric sewn around the waist to finish the upper raw edge and support the weight of the garment comfortably
A wide leather belt worn around the waist with a heavy metal buckle
A ribbon tied around the neck like a formal bowtie
An elastic band wrapped around a box of paper patterns
8.explanation: Constructed with crisp non-roll interfacing, waistbands anchor skirts and trousers firmly at the anatomical waist, distributing garment drape.

8.question: What is an 'elasticated casing'?
options: A fabric tunnel formed by folding over an edge or sewing an applied strip, through which elastic is threaded to draw the garment snugly to the body
A metal frame built around an industrial overlocker machine
A wooden trunk used to pack finished garments for overseas export
A plastic box used to store sewing machine needles safely
8.explanation: Simple folded or applied tunnels house elastic bands, providing adjustable, flexible comfort in casual pants, pyjamas, and sportswear.

8.question: What is a 'facing' in garment finishing?
options: Standing face-to-face with a customer in a tailor shop
Looking at yourself in a mirror while trying on a coat
A piece of fabric cut to the exact shape of an open raw edge (like a neckline or armhole) and stitched right sides together, then turned inside to finish the edge
Painting the face of a mannequin with makeup cosmetics
8.explanation: Internal facings finish raw edges cleanly without visible face stitching, providing crisp body when stabilized with fusible interfacing.

8.question: What is a 'shaped facing' (fitted facing)?
options: A facing cut out using a pattern piece that matches the exact shape and grainline of the garment edge being finished (e.g. curved neckline)
A square piece of cloth sewn into the corner of a pocket
A straight strip of fabric pulled tightly around a corner
A piece of cardboard cut into the shape of a human face
8.explanation: Cutting the facing on identical grain coordinates ensures identical expansion, prevent rolling, and maintains curved neckline contours.

8.question: What is an 'all-in-one facing' (combination facing)?
options: A single continuous facing piece that finishes both the neckline and both armholes of a sleeveless bodice in one clean operation
A sewing machine that weaves, dyes, cuts, and sews clothes at once
A single thread that sews an entire evening dress without cutting
A garment that combines a hat, coat, pants, and shoes in one piece
8.explanation: Combined neckline-armscye facings eliminate bulky separate seams in narrow shoulder straps on sleeveless tops and shift dresses.

8.question: What is an 'extended facing' (grown-on facing)?
options: A facing made by gluing three separate fabric scraps together
A facing that extends all the way down to the floor like a train
A facing cut in one continuous piece with the garment front, folded back along the foldline to finish the edge (e.g. front button placket)
A facing made from heavy thick leather on a silk blouse
8.explanation: Cutting front bands integral with the bodice eliminates a bulky seam along the center-front button closure, speeding up assembly.

8.question: What is a 'collar stand' on a shirt collar?
options: A wooden stand used to display shirts in department store windows
A plastic hook used to hang shirts on clotheslines to dry
A separate, upright curved band of fabric that raises the folded collar leaf above the neckline to frame the throat neatly
A cardboard strip inserted into a new shirt to keep it flat in stores
8.explanation: The collar stand elevates the folded collar fall cleanly over tailored suit lapels, providing structured support for neckties.

8.question: What is a 'cuff' on a garment sleeve?
options: A finished band of fabric sewn onto the bottom edge of a sleeve, fastening around the wrist with buttons or snaps (or folded back)
A metal handcuff used by police officers on duty
The decorative pocket sewn onto the left chest of a jacket
A tear ripped into the elbow of a denim work shirt
8.explanation: Cuffs gather sleeve volume neatly at the wrist, reinforced with interfacing and closed with plackets, buttons, or French cufflinks.

8.question: What is a 'sleeve placket' (such as a continuous lap or tailored shirt placket)?
options: A wooden plaque awarded to a tailor for fifty years of service
A metal plate screwed onto the front of a sewing machine
A finished opening at the cuff end of a sleeve that allows the hand to slip through comfortably before buttoning the cuff snugly
A plastic ruler used to measure sleeve lengths on paper patterns
8.explanation: Bound continuous laps or tailored gauntlet plackets bridge sleeve openings, preventing tearing when hands enter and exit cuffs.

8.question: What is a 'hem' on a garment?
options: The vertical seam running down the side of a jacket
The lower finished edge of a garment (skirt, dress, pants, sleeve) turned up and secured to prevent fraying and provide clean weight
A small plastic tag pinned to the sleeve displaying the price
The opening at the neck where the head passes through
8.explanation: Hems establish garment length and terminal drape weight, stabilized through blind stitching, machine topstitching, or fused webbing.

8.question: What is a 'double-turned hem' (machine-stitched hem)?
options: Sewing two separate dresses together at their bottom hems
Turning a garment inside out two times before putting it on
Folding the raw edge under twice (e.g. 6 mm then 1.5 cm) and machine stitching close to the inner folded edge, fully enclosing raw edges
Ironing a hem with two different household pressing irons
8.explanation: Standard for shirts, jeans, and lightweight cottons; dual folds conceal raw edges securely within a washable, topstitched hem band.

8.question: What is a 'blind-stitched hem' (invisible hem)?
options: A hem sewn in a completely dark room without turning on the lights
A hem secured with subtle hand or machine stitches that catch only a tiny thread of the outer fabric, remaining virtually invisible on the face
A hem glued with thick black rubber cement that shows on the front
A hem sewn with eyes closed by a trained master tailor
8.explanation: Catching only single fibers from the fashion face ensures tailored trousers and wool skirts display pristine, unbroken exterior drape.

8.question: What is a 'rolled hem' and on what fabrics is it used?
options: A thick hem rolled around a wooden rolling pin in the kitchen
A very narrow, delicate hem where the raw edge is rolled tightly and stitched with tiny hand stitches or overlocked; used on sheer silks and scarves
A heavy hem sewn on winter denim jeans with thick carpet thread
A hem made by rolling fabric into a ball and tying it with string
8.explanation: Hand-rolled edges or 3-thread rolled serging finish edges on delicate chiffon, organza, and foulard silk scarves without stiffening the drape.

8.question: What is a 'curved hem' and why must it be kept narrow?
options: A hem that is sewn crookedly by an untrained beginner sewer
A hem with a rounded contour (like a circular skirt); it must be kept narrow (approx. 6–12 mm) to prevent excess fabric bunching in the fold
A hem cut with jagged pinking shears along the bottom edge
A hem that curves upward over the shoulders like a collar
8.explanation: Because the circumference of the turned-up hem allowance is larger than the garment body, wide allowances ripple and pucker uncontrollably.

8.question: What is an 'in-seam pocket' (side-seam pocket)?
options: A pocket sewn onto the inside lining of a winter overcoat
A pocket sewn onto the outside knee of a pair of pants
A clear plastic pocket sewn onto the chest of a raincoat
A discreet pocket sewn into the side seam of a skirt, dress, or trousers, completely concealed inside the garment when not in use
8.explanation: Concealed pocket bags stitched to front and back side seam allowances rest smoothly within internal side margins without interrupting exterior lines.

8.question: What is a 'patch pocket'?
options: A patch sewn over a torn hole in the knee of garden pants
A secret pocket sewn inside the waistband of a pair of trousers
A pocket cut from fabric, turned under along edges, and topstitched directly onto the outside face of a garment (e.g. on jeans or safari jackets)
A pocket made by sewing ten tiny fabric scraps together
8.explanation: Topstitched surface pockets (flat, pleated, or bellowed) provide utilitarian storage and casual stylistic accents across workwear and blazers.

8.question: What is a 'welt pocket' (such as a jacket breast pocket)?
options: A pocket made from thick waterproof plastic sheet film
A pocket that hangs down from the bottom hem of a dress
A deep pocket sewn onto the knee of military cargo pants
A tailored pocket cut into the garment body, finished with one or two narrow fabric bands (welts) framing a clean horizontal or slanted slit opening
8.explanation: Single or double-besom welt pockets require precision slit cutting and internal stay reinforcement, characteristic of fine bespoke blazers.

8.question: What is 'basting' the pocket mouth closed during tailored jacket construction?
options: Gluing the pocket opening shut with hot melted wax
Sewing the pocket shut permanently so the wearer can never put hands inside
Temporary stitches holding the welt pocket mouth tightly shut during assembly and pressing, clipped open only after the garment is completely finished
Ironing the pocket with heavy starch until it cannot open
8.explanation: Basting prevents welt lips from sagging, distorting, or stretching out of alignment during subsequent pressing and handling operations.

8.question: What is an 'interfacing' applied to a patch pocket hem?
options: A strip of fusible interfacing applied to the top pocket hem fold to provide crisp firmness and prevent the opening from stretching out of shape
A piece of metal plate screwed inside the pocket to stop bullets
A decorative lace ribbon sewn around the bottom pocket curves
A soft cotton ball placed inside the pocket to keep hands warm
8.explanation: Fusible web across the pocket hem prevents unsightly stretching and distortion from repeated hand insertion during everyday wear.

8.question: What is a 'fly front zipper' on trousers and jeans?
options: A zipper that flies through the air when you pull the slider
A zipper sewn onto the back collar of an evening dress
A concealed zipper closure hidden beneath a protective fabric flap (fly shield and facing) running down the center front of pants
A zipper used to close a commercial fabric shopping bag
8.explanation: An underlay shield protects skin and underwear from metal teeth, while the topstitched J-stitch secures the outer facing neatly.

8.question: What is 'grading' (clipping) a neckline seam allowance before understitching?
options: Scoring a seam allowance test with a red grading pen
Trimming the facing allowance narrower than the garment allowance and clipping curves, ensuring the edge turns under cleanly without a bulky ridge
Measuring the width of the seam allowance with a wooden yardstick
Washing the seam allowance with laundry detergent to clean it
8.explanation: Tiered trimming and concave clipping release internal curvature tension, allowing the enclosed seam to roll inward unseen.

8.question: What is a 'godet' in skirt construction?
options: A triangular piece of fabric inserted into a slit or seam of a skirt to add flare, volume, and dynamic movement around the lower hem
A small plastic button sewn onto a shirt cuff
A decorative embroidery stitch used to hem tablecloths
A metal snap fastener used to close jacket collars
8.explanation: Inserting triangular fabric godets expands the lower hem circumference, creating dramatic fluted sweeps while keeping hips form-fitted.

8.question: What is a 'peplum' in skirt and jacket styling?
options: A long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist like a towel
A high hat worn by chefs working in restaurant kitchens
A short, flared or gathered flounce sewn at the waistline, flaring out over the hips to accentuate the waist
A pair of leather boots worn with winter overcoats
8.explanation: Waist-seam peplums emphasize feminine hourglass silhouettes, flaring outward over the iliac crests to contrast waist suppression.

8.question: What is a 'kick pleat' (vent) on the back of a pencil skirt or tailored jacket?
options: A place where the tailor kicked the garment across the floor
A pleat sewn into the side seam of running sports shorts
A decorative ruffle sewn around the bottom hem of a dress
An overlapping opening or inverted pleat at the bottom hem that provides ease of movement for walking while maintaining a sleek silhouette
8.explanation: Vents and kick pleats accommodate striding leg extension and sitting ergonomics without causing narrow pencil skirts to ride up.

8.question: What is 'easing' a seam in garment construction?
options: Cutting off half of the fabric allowance with scissors
Loosening the tension discs on a sewing machine completely
Taking a nap on a sofa after finishing a sewing project
Joining a slightly longer edge of fabric to a slightly shorter edge smoothly without creating visible gathers, tucks, or puckers (e.g. sleeve head)
8.explanation: Subtle differential feeding molds three-dimensional fullness into convex armholes and shoulder seams without puckering.

8.question: What is a 'rouleau loop' (spaghetti loop)?
options: A thick plastic rope used to tie cargo boxes onto trucks
A narrow, bias-cut fabric tube turned right side out, formed into loops and inserted into seams to act as buttonholes for tiny round buttons
A heavy metal chain used to hang coats on display racks
A bowl of Italian pasta eaten during tailor lunch breaks
8.explanation: Turned bias tubes form elegant loops along bridal and couture button plackets, framing delicate self-covered shank buttons.

8.question: What is a 'scalloped edge' in garment finishing?
options: A decorative finished edge formed of continuous repeating semicircular curved shapes (scallops), commonly faced and turned on hems and collars
An edge cut with jagged pinking shears in a straight line
A seafood dinner served in luxury hotel restaurants
An edge that has been torn by a dog biting the hem
8.explanation: Convex repeating semicircles require precision needle pivoting, notch clipping, and careful pressing to roll crisp convex contours.

8.question: What is 'fusing' interfacing with a household iron?
options: Washing fabric in boiling water until the glue washes away
Sticking fabric pieces together with liquid paper glue
Applying heat, steam, and firm downward pressure with an iron for 10–15 seconds per section without sliding the iron, melting resin glue to fabric
Melting the fabric into liquid plastic with an open flame
8.explanation: Static vertical pressure and steam melt thermoplastic adhesive dots into fabric interstices; sliding irons displaces resin and wrinkles fabric.

8.question: Why must a fused fabric panel be allowed to COOL completely before moving or handling it?
options: Because the fabric will turn bright green if moved while warm
Because the sewer's fingers will freeze to the iron soleplate
Because the fabric will catch fire if touched while warm
The melted resin adhesive requires cooling time to set and solidify permanently; moving it while warm breaks the adhesive bond
8.explanation: Thermoplastic polymers achieve full shear bonding strength only upon crystallizing at ambient temperatures; premature flex causes bubbling.

9.question: What are 'fastenings' in garment design?
options: Mechanical devices or components (such as zippers, buttons, snaps, hooks) used to close, open, and secure garment openings comfortably
Ropes used to tie delivery trucks to shipping docks
Safety pins used to pin cardboard price tags onto coats
Belts worn around the waist with decorative metal buckles
9.explanation: Fastenings enable garments to pass over wider body circumferences (shoulders, hips) before closing snugly around smaller anatomical contours.

9.question: What is a 'standard coil zipper' (nylon zipper)?
options: A zipper that has no teeth and closes using liquid magnetic glue
A heavy zipper made with individually cast brass metal teeth
A lightweight, flexible zipper featuring continuous spiraled nylon/polyester monofilament coils stitched to woven side tapes
A zipper with giant plastic teeth used on heavy winter coats
9.explanation: Flexible polyester coil zips bend easily around contours, resisting tooth dislodgement and proving ideal for skirts, dresses, and knitwear.

9.question: What is an 'invisible zipper' (concealed zipper)?
options: A zipper whose coils are turned to the reverse side, concealed within the seamline so only the narrow teardrop pull tab is visible on the outside
A zipper made of completely transparent glass that cannot be seen
A zipper that closes automatically without pulling the slider
A zipper sewn without any thread using invisible radio waves
9.explanation: Inwardly rolled teeth rest concealed behind folded seam lips, producing an unbroken, sleek exterior seamline on evening wear and skirts.

9.question: What is a 'separating zipper' (open-ended zipper)?
options: A zipper sewn around the bottom circular hem of a skirt
A zipper designed to detach completely at the bottom with a pin and box mechanism (e.g. used on jackets and cardigans)
A zipper that breaks into pieces when you pull on it
A zipper used exclusively to close luggage suitcases
9.explanation: Separating retainers permit jacket front panels to pull apart completely when unzipped, locking together securely via insertion pins.

9.question: What is a 'shank button'?
options: A flat button with two or four holes drilled straight through the face
A button made of soft foam rubber that squashes completely flat
A button carved from a piece of sharp volcanic glass
A button with a solid decorative face and a raised loop, hole, or stem underneath (the shank) that elevates the button above the fabric
9.explanation: The hollow under-shank provides elevation, accommodating the thickness of heavy coat fabric layers beneath the buttonhole without pulling.

9.question: What is a 'flat button' (sew-through button)?
options: A button that has a heavy metal shank stem on the back
A flat disc button with two or four holes drilled through the center, sewn directly through the holes to the fabric
A button shaped like a hollow three-dimensional sphere
A button that snaps together using magnetic force
9.explanation: Standard 2-hole and 4-hole flat buttons lie close to fabric surfaces, suited for shirts, blouses, and lightweight apparel closures.

9.question: Why should a 'thread shank' be created when hand-sewing a flat button onto a heavy wool coat?
options: To use up extra thread left over from sewing seams
To create a stem that elevates the button, allowing the thick wool buttonhole layer to sit smoothly underneath without puckering
To prevent the button from changing colour in sunlight
To make the button rotate like a propeller when walking
9.explanation: Wrapping thread around connecting strands forms an artificial shank, providing vertical clearance for thick tailored coat fronts.

9.question: How is a thread shank created during hand-sewing of a flat button?
options: Sew through the button using an industrial steel wire staple
Tie ten knots on top of the button with heavy fishing line
Place a matchstick or toothpick over the button between the holes while sewing, remove it, pull the button up, and wind thread tightly around the stitches underneath
Glue a small wooden block underneath the button with hot glue
9.explanation: A spacer matchstick provides controlled slack; withdrawing it allows the sewist to wind tight thread wraps around the neck to form a rigid shank.

9.question: What is a 'hook and eye' fastening?
options: A pair of plastic safety goggles worn in cutting rooms
A fishing hook used to catch freshwater fish in rivers
A two-part metal closure consisting of a curved wire hook that latches into a matching wire loop (eye), providing a secure, discreet closure at seam tops
A pair of eyeglasses worn by tailors while hand-sewing
9.explanation: Small wire hooks and round eyes (or flat straight bars) secure waistband extensions and zipper tops against lateral shear stress.

9.question: What is the difference between a 'wire eye' (round eye) and a 'straight eye' (bar eye)?
options: A round eye is sewn on shoes; a bar eye is sewn on hats
A round wire eye is used where edges overlap or abut; a straight bar eye is used where edges overlap flatly (like on waistbands)
A round eye dissolves in water; a bar eye lasts forever
A round eye is made of wood; a bar eye is made of plastic
9.explanation: Round loop eyes accept hooks across butted neckline edges; flat bar eyes lie flush under overlapping waistband tabs without bulging.

9.question: What is a 'snap fastener' (press stud / popper)?
options: A heavy zipper that pulls shut in less than one second
A magnetic strip that sticks to metal refrigerators
A strip of Velcro that pulls apart with loud ripping noises
A two-piece metal or plastic fastening consisting of a ball (stud) component that snaps firmly into a socket component under gentle finger pressure
9.explanation: Ball-and-socket closures provide flat, discreet, low-stress closures along overlapping facings, cuffs, and baby bodysuits.

9.question: Which part of a snap fastener should be sewn to the upper (overlapping) garment layer?
options: The raised 'ball' (stud) component
Neither part; snap fasteners are sewn only on the inside lining
Both parts must be glued to the upper layer simultaneously
The flatter 'socket' part (to prevent the ball from showing as an unsightly bump on the garment face)
9.explanation: Sewing the smooth, concave socket to the overlap hides the profile, while the projecting ball stud mounts flush on the underlap.

9.question: What is 'hook-and-loop' fastening (Velcro)?
options: A pair of metal hooks connected by an elastic rubber cord
A wooden toggle button tied with a leather cord loop
A fastening consisting of two woven nylon tapes: one covered in microscopic stiff hooks, and the other covered in soft hairy loops that stick together
A metal zipper sewn onto the front opening of a winter coat
9.explanation: Pressing tiny molded hooks against fibrous loops creates strong shear resistance, opening easily under peel tension on shoes and cuffs.

9.question: What is an advantage of hook-and-loop fastening (Velcro) in adaptive and children's clothing?
options: It makes garments completely fireproof against high heat
It is quick, easy, and intuitive to open and close, ideal for individuals with limited manual dexterity or young children who cannot tie or button
It is completely invisible from both sides of the garment
It can be pressed with an extremely hot iron without melting
9.explanation: High accessibility eliminates fine-motor buttoning demands, empowering young children, elderly, and disabled individuals with independence.

9.question: What is a potential disadvantage of hook-and-loop fastening in everyday laundering?
options: It turns into solid steel metal after being washed with soap
It makes the washing machine stop spinning permanently
The stiff hooks can snag, pull, and damage delicate adjacent fabrics (like knits and lace) in the wash, and lint clogs the hooks over time
It dissolves into thin air when exposed to cold tap water
9.explanation: Exposed hook tapes abrade knit filaments and attract laundry lint, progressively degrading peel adhesion if not fastened prior to washing.

9.question: What is a 'toggle' fastening?
options: A magnetic snap that clicks shut inside a leather purse
An elongated, cylindrical button (often made of wood, horn, or plastic) secured through a cord, leather loop, or rope loop (classic on duffle coats)
A flat round metal disc with four holes in the middle
A small metal hook that slips into an embroidered eye
9.explanation: Elongated barrels slip through thick rope or leather frog loops, designed historically for easy fastening while wearing thick naval gloves.

9.question: What is a 'frog' closure (Chinese frog)?
options: A metal zipper painted with green waterproof enamel paint
An ornamental braided fabric cord fastening consisting of an intricate knot on one side that fastens through a matching cord loop on the other
A live green frog placed in the pocket of a summer jacket
A pair of heavy tailoring shears used to cut thick denim
9.explanation: Elaborate tubular bias-cording knotted into trefoils and mandalas provides high ornamental closure on cheongsams, tuxedos, and military tunics.

9.question: What is 'grommet' (or eyelet) hardware in garments?
options: A metal coin sewn inside the hem of a coat to add weight
A metal or plastic reinforcement ring set into a punched hole in fabric, used for threading laces, ribbons, or cords (e.g. on corsets, hoodies, sneakers)
A plastic button sewn onto the cuff of a tailored shirt
A small round mirror glued to the chest of a party dress
9.explanation: Two-piece flared metal rings clamp fabric margins around punched holes, preventing hole fraying under intense tensile cord pulling.

9.question: What is an 'eyelet' formed by hand embroidery?
options: A small circular hole punched through fabric and reinforced around its perimeter with dense, tight buttonhole or satin stitches
A pair of reading glasses worn by tailor assistants
A metal zipper sewn onto the front fly of a pair of jeans
A plastic bead sewn onto the front of an evening dress
9.explanation: Stiletto awls expand warp/weft yarns without cutting fibers; dense radial buttonhole stitches encase the circular perimeter smoothly.

9.question: What is a 'magnetic snap' closure?
options: A metal button that changes colour when touched by magnets
A concealed two-piece closure with built-in neodymium magnets that snap together automatically when brought close, commonly used in bags and coats
A snap that repels all clothing items made of cotton
A snap that attracts lightning bolts during summer storms
9.explanation: Magnetic flux draws opposing poles together automatically, offering effortless, blind closure on handbag flaps and adaptive outerwear.

9.question: What is a 'lapped zipper' application?
options: A zipper sewn onto the lapel of a winter overcoat
A zipper that laps around the waist three times like a belt
A zipper that has been accidentally sewn upside down
A zipper insertion method where one folded edge of fabric completely overlaps and conceals the zipper teeth from view (common in side seams and skirts)
9.explanation: The front edge laps 1.2 cm over the zipper teeth, providing a clean tailored flap that hides teeth while allowing smooth slider transit.

9.question: What is a 'centered zipper' (railroad zipper) application?
options: A zipper insertion method where the zipper teeth are centered directly under the seamline, with two equal folds meeting over the center teeth
A zipper installed along the tracks of a toy train set
A zipper sewn down the exact center of a wooden table
A zipper that has teeth on only one side of the tape
9.explanation: Two symmetrical 6 mm topstitching rows parallel the seam on either side, forming balanced railroad tracks common on center back dress closures.

9.question: What is an 'exposed zipper' application in modern fashion?
options: A broken zipper that cannot be closed by the wearer
A zipper sewn on the inside lining of a winter coat
A zipper whose teeth have been pulled off with pliers
A decorative zipper insertion where the metal or contrasting plastic teeth and tape are deliberately visible on the outside of the garment
9.explanation: Bold metallic brass or colored plastic teeth sit proudly on the garment face, functioning simultaneously as closures and industrial design accents.

9.question: What is a 'two-way zipper' (dual slider zipper)?
options: A zipper that has teeth on both the inside and outside
A zipper that can only be pulled shut by two people at once
A zipper equipped with two separate sliders that can be opened from the bottom as well as the top, allowing comfortable sitting in long coats
A zipper that breaks in half after being used two times
9.explanation: Dual opposing sliders allow long parkas to unzip from the bottom hem, providing leg mobility for walking, driving, and sitting.

9.question: What is a 'button loop' made of elastic cord or thread?
options: A button that has been crushed flat by an electric iron
A decorative embroidery stitch used to hem bedsheets
A loop of heavy steel wire used to hang coats on display racks
A loop of cord, elastic, or self-fabric sewn into a seam to slip over a button instead of cutting a traditional buttonhole slit
9.explanation: Loop fastenings slip over round shank or pearl buttons, eliminating fabric slitting on delicate bridal bodices and keyhole back necklines.

9.question: What is an 'interlining' in winter outerwear?
options: A strip of plastic tape glued along the bottom hem of a dress
A warm insulating fabric layer (such as fleece, thinsulate, or down batting) sewn between the outer shell fabric and the inner lining for warmth
A decorative lace ribbon sewn onto the collar of a blouse
A piece of cardboard placed inside the shoulders of a jacket
9.explanation: Lofted synthetic batting or down fills the interstitial chamber, trapping quiescent air to insulate against conductive environmental heat loss.

9.question: What is 'shoulder pad' in tailoring?
options: A plastic badge pinned to the shoulder displaying the brand logo
A soft pillow carried by tailors to sleep on during breaks
A piece of leather sewn onto the elbow of a tweed jacket
A shaped, tapered wedge of batting or foam inserted into the shoulder head of a jacket or dress to define, level, and support the shoulder silhouette
9.explanation: Layered cotton fleece or molded polyurethane pads square anatomical slope lines, providing an elevated bridge for crisp sleeve head drape.

9.question: What is a 'sleeve head roll' (sleeve head wadding) in tailored jackets?
options: A strip of bias-cut fleece or hair canvas sewn into the upper sleeve seam allowance to prevent the sleeve cap from dimpling or collapsing
A wooden rolling pin used to press jacket sleeves flat
A heavy metal cylinder used to test fabric strength
A roll of paper towels used to clean tailoring irons
9.explanation: Inserted inside the armscye cap, the lofted fleece strip supports the sleeve cap curve, eliminating hollow indentations below the shoulder pad.

9.question: What is 'hair canvas' (horsehair canvas) in bespoke tailoring?
options: A paintbrush used to paint portraits of horses in studios
A piece of fur harvested from wild animal pelts for collars
A rough piece of sandpaper used to scrub denim jackets
A resilient, springy woven canvas made with animal hair (horsehair/goat hair) and wool, used inside tailored suit jackets to create lasting chest structure
9.explanation: High flexural recovery from animal hair fibers provides permanent three-dimensional chest canvas roll without stiff artificial adhesives.

9.question: What is 'boning' in corsetry and evening gowns?
options: Real animal bones sewn into the hem of winter coats to add weight
Carving buttons out of dry cattle bones with handheld chisels
A culinary technique where meat bones are boiled to make soup
Rigid or flexible strips (steel or plastic Rigilene) inserted into internal fabric channels to support, shape, and maintain vertical tension in strapless garments
9.explanation: Flexible spiral steel or feather-light polyester bones resist longitudinal compression, preventing strapless bodices from collapsing around the torso.

9.question: What is 'waist stay' (grosgrain stay) in formal dresses?
options: A metal wire wrapped tightly around the waist like a belt
A piece of elastic rubber band sewn into the cuffs of sleeves
A wide leather belt worn on the outside of winter coats
A strong, non-stretch grosgrain ribbon sewn inside the waist of a strapless or heavy dress, anchored around the body to bear the garment's weight
9.explanation: Snug interior grosgrain bands anchor gown mass directly onto the pelvic iliac crest, preventing heavy skirts from dragging strapless bodices down.

9.question: What is 'bias tape' (bias binding)?
options: Heavy masking tape used to hold paper patterns onto tables
Clear scotch tape used to repair torn pattern tissue sheets
Strips of fabric cut diagonally at 45 degrees to the selvedge, with pre-folded edges, used to bind raw edges or form decorative trims
Sticky plastic packaging tape used to seal cardboard boxes
9.explanation: Diagonal elasticity allows pre-folded bias tapes to curve effortlessly around concave necklines and convex hems without wrinkling.

9.question: What is 'piping cord'?
options: A plastic tube used to blow compressed air across cutting tables
A thin nylon thread used to sew buttonholes on shirts
A soft, round cotton or polyester cord enclosed inside a bias fabric strip to create dimensional raised piping along garment edges and seams
A metal electrical wire used to plug sewing machines into walls
9.explanation: Enclosed within bias strips, dimensional cotton cords provide structural definition, abrasion resistance, and crisp accent lines to upholstery and lapels.

9.question: What is 'seam tape' (stay tape)?
options: Adhesive paper tape used to wrap shipping parcels
Heavy black electrical tape wrapped around machine wires
A narrow, stable, non-stretch woven twill tape or ribbon sewn into bias seams (like shoulder seams) to prevent them from stretching out of shape
A strip of clear scotch tape stuck onto sewing machine tables
9.explanation: Stitched along shoulder seams and pocket mouths, pre-shrunk cotton stay tape locks longitudinal grain dimensions, preventing permanent stretching.

9.question: What is 'rick-rack' braid?
options: A jagged tear ripped into the side seam of a skirt
A broken wooden chair sitting in the corner of a sewing shop
A metal tool used to pull zippers shut when stuck
A decorative, flat woven zigzag trimming braid used to ornament children's clothing, aprons, collars, and hems
9.explanation: Woven serpentine braid provides vintage visual rhythm and colorful border trims, easily stitched along outer garment margins without fraying.

9.question: What is 'lace trim'?
options: A heavy rope used to tie shoes tightly for running
A piece of thick plastic used to waterproof jacket seams
A flat strip of leather used to manufacture belts
An openwork, decorative patterned fabric trim (narrow band) with open holes, used to embellish necklines, hemlines, and lingerie
9.explanation: Delicate openwork borders (Chantilly, Guipure, Cluny) frame hems and necklines with intricate floral transparency and tactile femininity.

9.question: What is 'fringe' trimming?
options: Cutting human hair bangs straight across the forehead
A row of metal buttons sewn along the sleeve cuff
An ornamental textile border of hanging loose threads, cords, or tassels, commonly used on shawls, jackets, and evening wear
The small brand label sewn inside the collar of a jacket
9.explanation: Loose hanging yarn ends or looped tassels add dynamic kinetic movement, acoustic rustle, and tactile texture to western jackets and dancewear.

9.question: What is a 'tassel' in decorative trimmings?
options: A metal pin used to hold paper patterns onto fabric
A wooden spool around which sewing thread is wound
A hanging ornament made by binding a bunch of cords or threads together at one end, leaving the lower ends loose (e.g. on cushions, ties, robes)
A small plastic button sewn onto the cuff of a shirt
9.explanation: Tufted thread bundles gathered beneath an ornamental wrapped neck form opulent pendants on graduation caps, cushion corners, and sash ties.

9.question: What is 'sequin trim'?
options: A string of dried beans used to count sewing stitches
A row of plain wooden buttons sewn along a coat seam
A continuous ribbon or string of overlapping, shiny plastic discs (sequins) pre-stitched together, sewn onto garments for sparkle
A strip of clear plastic packaging tape with zero shine
9.explanation: Pre-strung holographic or metallic PVC paillettes sewn in continuous chain-stitch ribbons deliver rapid, dazzling sparkle to dance costumes.

9.question: What is 'beaded trim'?
options: A row of dry peas sewn into the seam of a blanket
A necklace worn around the neck during evening parties
A string of metal nuts and bolts used to repair machines
A narrow decorative band or fringe pre-strung with glass beads, pearls, or bugle beads, designed to be stitched onto hems or necklines
9.explanation: Faceted glass seed beads and bugles pre-assembled onto textile ribbon carriers provide luxurious weight and light-catching elegance to evening wear.

9.question: What is a 'buckle' on a garment belt?
options: A metal or plastic clasp consisting of a frame and prong used for fastening two loose ends of a belt or strap firmly together
A flat button with four holes drilled through the face
A metal zipper sewn onto the front opening of a jacket
A small metal hook that slips into an embroidered eye
9.explanation: Tongue prongs and rectangular frames clamp perforated strap webbing, providing adjustable girth retention on trench coats and overalls.

9.question: What is 'elastic webbing'?
options: A strong, flat, woven or knitted strip of elastic rubber yarns, used in waistbands, athletic cuffs, and suspenders for snug stretch fit
A piece of clear plastic tape used to wrap shipping parcels
A net used by fishermen to catch wild salmon in rivers
A spider web collected from the corners of sewing rooms
9.explanation: High-modulus elastomeric core yarns braided with polyester sheath fibers provide firm longitudinal recovery in activewear and underwear bands.

9.question: What is 'drawstring' cord?
options: A narrow cord, rope, or fabric ribbon threaded through an enclosed casing, pulled and tied to cinch a waistband, hood, or hem
A wire cable used to pull elevators up in buildings
A string of metal keys used to unlock factory doors
A thread used to sew buttonholes onto tailored shirts
9.explanation: Internal drawstrings terminate through metal eyelets, allowing wearers to manually tighten or loosen hood and athletic pant apertures.

9.question: What is a 'cord lock' (cord stopper / toggle stopper)?
options: A tool used to sharpen blunt tailoring scissors
A heavy brass lock used to secure tailoring studio doors
A plastic pin used to hold paper patterns onto tables
A spring-loaded plastic cylinder that slides along a drawstring cord to lock it firmly in place without needing to tie a knot
9.explanation: Internal coiled steel springs pinch cords against plastic barrel apertures, providing one-handed cinch adjustments on backpacks and jackets.

9.question: What is 'hem tape' (lace hem tape)?
options: Sticky scotch tape used to wrap Christmas presents
Clear plastic packaging tape used to seal cardboard boxes
A narrow, woven rayon or lace ribbon stitched to the raw edge of a hem allowance before hand-hemming, preventing fraying without bulky folds
Heavy masking tape used to hold fabric rolls onto trucks
9.explanation: Stitching supple, non-bulky lace ribbon along hem margins covers raw edges cleanly on heavy wool skirts without requiring a double fold.

9.question: What are 'covered buttons' (self-covered buttons)?
options: Buttons that have been covered in liquid candle wax
Buttons hidden underneath a blanket so nobody can see them
Buttons painted with thick black house paint
Buttons constructed using metal or plastic button shells wrapped and covered in the garment's matching fashion fabric
9.explanation: Specialized two-piece metal blanks crimp circles of fashion cloth tightly, producing monochromatic, custom-matched couture buttoning.

9.question: What is a 'shank former' (spacer) used during hand button sewing?
options: A hammer used to crush metal buttons on tailoring tables
A plastic bottle used to hold liquid machine oil
A small flat tool (or toothpick/pin) inserted under the button while hand-stitching to ensure uniform thread shank height
A sharp pair of scissors used to cut buttonholes open
9.explanation: Standardized thickness spacers ensure repeatable clearance under every button, matching the precise thickness of the overlapping buttonhole band.

9.question: What is 'iron-on mending tape'?
options: A woven fabric tape coated with dry hot-melt adhesive on one side, used to patch and repair tears or holes in garments from the reverse
Sticky paper tape used to wrap parcels for shipping
A band of electrical tape wrapped around machine wires
Clear scotch tape used to repair torn paper money notes
9.explanation: Fused over tears on the garment reverse, thermal adhesive webs stabilize torn fabric edges without requiring visible exterior surface stitching.

9.question: What is 'casing elastic' (non-roll elastic)?
options: A firm, rib-knit or woven elastic band engineered with vertical ribs that resist rolling, twisting, or folding over inside a garment waistband
A thin nylon thread used to sew sheer silk evening dresses
A piece of rubber band that curls into a tight ball when pulled
A heavy steel wire cable used to anchor cargo ships
9.explanation: Transverse monofilament ribs provide vertical stiffness, preventing waistband elastics from curling or rolling inside fabric channels.

9.question: What is 'applique scissors' (duckbill scissors)?
options: Scissors shaped like a real living duck that quacks when cutting
Scissors painted bright yellow used by children in kindergarten
Specialized scissors with a wide, paddle-shaped 'duckbill' blade that shields the base fabric while closely trimming appliqué or lace edges
Heavy industrial shears used to cut sheet metal plates
9.explanation: The broad, flat duckbill paddle rests flat against base cloth, deflecting it away while the upper pointed blade shears appliqué margins cleanly.

10.question: What is 'Fast Fashion' in the modern global textile industry?
options: Traditional cultural clothing that lasts for over fifty years
Clothing designed specifically for Olympic sprint athletes
A garment that is sewn in less than five seconds by robots
A retail business model based on rapidly mass-producing cheap, trend-led disposable clothing with fast inventory turnover and low retail prices
10.explanation: Rapid design-to-rack cycles (1–2 weeks) stimulate hyper-consumption, driving acute environmental degradation and exploitative labor.

10.question: What is 'Slow Fashion'?
options: A sustainable, ethical fashion movement advocating for high quality, durable design, fair worker wages, and mindful, reduced consumption
Wearing clothes that are three sizes too large for you
Taking three hours to put on your clothes in the morning
A fashion style that uses only snail shells for buttons
10.explanation: Slow fashion champions artisan craftsmanship, classic timeless silhouettes, transparent supply chains, and circular resource stewardship.

10.question: What is an environmental impact of excessive synthetic garment consumption in the fashion industry?
options: Massive petroleum resource depletion, greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing, and microplastic pollution in global waterways
The permanent cooling of global ocean temperatures by five degrees
The total elimination of all solid waste from municipal landfills
An instant decrease in atmospheric carbon dioxide levels
10.explanation: Synthetics emit ~3 times more CO2 per kilogram than cotton and shed millions of non-biodegradable microfibres into marine food chains.

10.question: How do synthetic textile garments contribute to oceanic 'microplastic' pollution?
options: Buttons fall off shirts and turn into gold dust in the sea
During domestic machine washing, friction causes synthetic clothes (polyester, nylon, acrylic) to shed microscopic plastic fibres that pass through sewage plants into oceans
Garment factories throw plastic sewing machines into rivers
Zippers dissolve in cold water and turn into salt crystals
10.explanation: A single wash load can release >700,000 microplastic filaments, which evade municipal filtration and bioaccumulate in trophic marine webs.

10.question: What is 'textile recycling'?
options: Throwing all unwanted clothes into the municipal garbage bin
The process of recovering and processing discarded post-industrial fabric offcuts or post-consumer clothing into new materials or products
Dyeing an old shirt with dark black ink to hide food stains
Wearing dirty clothes without washing them for three months
10.explanation: Diverting textiles from landfills, mechanical shredding (shoddy) or chemical depolymerization regenerates spun yarns and insulation materials.

10.question: What is 'mechanical textile recycling'?
options: Ironing clothes with an automated computerized pressing iron
Dissolving fabric in chemical acid to make liquid paint
Cutting fabric into tiny paper confetti with tailoring shears
Shredding, pulling, and tearing fabrics apart into loose fibres to be carded and re-spun into new yarns (often yielding shorter, weaker fibres)
10.explanation: Garnetting and garnett machines tear knitted/woven rags into staple fibers, whose reduced fiber length typically requires virgin carrier blending.

10.question: What is 'chemical textile recycling'?
options: Dipping old clothes into boiling household bleach barrels
Burning clothes in open barrels to make black charcoal dust
Depolymerizing textile waste (e.g. polyester or cotton) back into its fundamental chemical monomers, purifying them, and re-extruding virgin-quality fibres
Spraying clothes with perfume so they smell clean without washing
10.explanation: Glycolysis and enzymatic digestion break polymers down into pristine terephthalic acid or cellulose dope, achieving closed-loop infinite recycling.

10.question: What is 'upcycling' in sustainable fashion design?
options: Throwing away five shirts to buy one expensive new jacket
Transforming discarded clothing, textile offcuts, or waste materials into new garments or accessories of higher aesthetic or commercial value
Burying old clothes in garden compost soil behind a house
Riding a bicycle up a steep mountain highway in the rain
10.explanation: Creative deconstruction and reconstructive tailoring elevate post-consumer waste into unique, high-value artistic garments.
