10.question: What is 'zero-waste pattern cutting'?
options: A fashion design that has no sleeves, no collar, and no hem
Designing pattern pieces that fit together like a complete jigsaw puzzle on the fabric width, utilizing 100% of the cloth with zero scrap waste
Refusing to cut fabric and wrapping whole cloth bolts around the body
Sewing clothes without using any sewing thread or needles
10.explanation: Integrating garment aesthetics with mathematical marker layout eliminates the standard 15% fabric cutting room waste entirely.

10.question: What is 'organic cotton'?
options: Cotton woven exclusively on antique wooden handlooms
Cotton cultivated from non-genetically modified plants without the use of synthetic chemical pesticides, herbicides, or synthetic fertilisers
Cotton that grows without roots or water in dry desert sand
Cotton dyed exclusively with bright fluorescent chemical dyes
10.explanation: Certified organic farming (GOTS) relies on crop rotation, beneficial insect predators, and compost, protecting farm soil and groundwater.

10.question: What does the 'Global Organic Textile Standard' (GOTS) certification assure consumers?
options: The clothing contains 100% pure artificial plastic fibres
The garment was manufactured inside a government military base
The textile contains at least 70–95% certified organic fibres, processed under strict environmental and social labor criteria across the entire supply chain
The garment was sewn entirely by hand by certified fashion designers
10.explanation: GOTS mandates zero toxic heavy-metal dyestuffs, wastewater treatment for wet processing, and compliance with ILO fair labor conventions.

10.question: What does the 'OEKO-TEX Standard 100' label certify on a garment?
options: Every component of the garment (fabric, threads, buttons, zippers, linings) has been rigorously tested and certified free from harmful levels of toxic chemicals
The garment will never wear out or tear for one hundred years
The garment was manufactured using 100% pure green solar energy
The clothing is completely fireproof against high-temperature fires
10.explanation: Independent laboratory testing verifies the absence of regulated azo dyes, nickel, formaldehyde, phthalates, and allergenic disperse dyestuffs.

10.question: What does a 'wash tub with a number' (e.g. 40°C) represent on an international textile care label?
options: The percentage of laundry soap detergent that must be added
The number of minutes the garment should be left in the washer
The number of times the garment can be washed before wearing out
The maximum recommended water temperature for machine washing the garment (e.g. wash at or below 40 degrees Celsius)
10.explanation: International ISO 3758 wash tub symbols specify maximum thermal wash limits to prevent fiber shrinkage, color bleeding, and elastane degradation.

10.question: What does a 'wash tub with a hand inside' signify on a garment care label?
options: You must wear rubber gloves when touching the clean garment
The garment must be washed by five people at the same time
Hand wash only; the garment is too delicate for mechanical machine washing (do not machine wash)
The garment is used exclusively as a kitchen dish hand towel
10.explanation: Delicate silks, fine wools, and beaded garments require gentle manual immersion without mechanical agitating paddles or high-speed spin cycles.

10.question: What does a 'triangle' symbol represent on a textile care label?
options: Bleaching instructions (e.g. empty triangle = any bleach allowed; triangle with diagonal lines = non-chlorine bleach only; crossed-out = do not bleach)
The garment is shaped like a pyramid or triangle
The garment must be ironed using an antique flat iron
The garment was manufactured in an Egyptian clothing factory
10.explanation: ISO standards reserve the equilateral triangle for oxidative bleaching protocols, distinguishing safe oxygen bleaches from damaging chlorine.

10.question: What does a 'circle inside a square' represent on an international care label?
options: The garment was manufactured on a circular knitting machine
The garment must be rolled into a ball and stored in a box
The garment must be dry cleaned in a commercial laundromat
Tumble drying instructions (e.g. one dot = low heat; two dots = medium heat; crossed out = do not tumble dry)
10.explanation: The square symbolizes domestic drying, while the inscribed circle indicates mechanical rotary drum tumble drying and thermal limit dots.

10.question: What does a 'flat clothes iron' symbol with ONE dot represent on a care label?
options: Iron with an iron that is heated over an open campfire
Iron the garment only once every ten years
Iron using three commercial irons at the same time
Iron at low temperature (maximum 110°C / 230°F), recommended for heat-sensitive synthetics like nylon and acrylic
10.explanation: One dot (110°C) protects low-melting-point synthetics; two dots (150°C) suits wool/polyester; three dots (200°C) handles cotton and linen.

10.question: What does a 'circle' symbol represent on an international textile care label?
options: The garment is designed exclusively for circular dancers
Professional textile care / dry cleaning instructions (e.g. 'P' inside = dry clean with perchloroethylene; crossed-out = do not dry clean)
The garment must be washed in cold water inside a round bucket
The garment must be rolled into a circle and hung on a wall
10.explanation: The plain circle designates professional solvent dry cleaning and wet cleaning protocols, with internal letters indicating chemical solvents.

10.question: What is 'dry cleaning' and how does it clean delicate garments?
options: Cleaning clothes by rubbing them with dry beach sand
Blowing high-pressure cold air across clothes with a fan
Cleaning textiles using an organic chemical liquid solvent (traditionally perchloroethylene - 'perc') instead of water and detergent
Hanging clothes in the hot desert sun to dry out stains
10.explanation: Non-aqueous solvent immersion dissolves oils and grease without swelling delicate hydrophilic wool/silk fibers, preventing dimensional shrinkage.

10.question: What is an environmental and occupational health concern regarding traditional 'perchloroethylene' (perc) dry cleaning?
options: Perc makes clothes smell like sweet fresh strawberries
Perc makes clothing turn bright neon yellow in sunlight
Perc causes garments to catch fire spontaneously in closets
Perc is a toxic, volatile organic compound, a suspected human carcinogen, and can contaminate groundwater and air if not recaptured
10.explanation: Toxicity and groundwater persistence have driven regulatory bans on tetrachloroethylene, prompting shifts to liquid CO2 and professional wet cleaning.

10.question: What is 'wet cleaning' as an eco-friendly alternative to chemical dry cleaning?
options: Spraying clothes with high-pressure garden hoses outdoors
Soaking clothes in a cold river for three days without soap
A professional, computer-controlled cleaning system using water, biodegradable detergents, and gentle mechanical agitation to safely clean 'dry clean only' fabrics
Throwing clothes into a swimming pool filled with chlorine
10.explanation: Advanced moisture sensors and delicate non-felting drum physics permit aqueous laundering of wool and silk without felting or fiber distortion.

10.question: What causes wool sweaters to shrink and become stiff and thick when washed incorrectly in hot water with agitation?
options: Felting: heat, moisture, and mechanical tumbling cause the directional cuticle scales on wool fibres to interlock and jam together permanently
The wool fibres evaporate into thin air during washing
Wool fibres absorb laundry detergent and turn into solid stone
Hot water melts the wool fibres into liquid plastic soup
10.explanation: The directional friction effect (DFE) ratchet mechanism drives overlapping scales past each other under agitation, locking fibres irreversibly.

10.question: How should fine woollen garments be dried after gentle washing to prevent stretching or misshaping?
options: Roll in a clean towel to remove excess water, then reshape and dry flat on a horizontal drying rack away from direct heat and sunlight
Tumble dry on the highest heat setting for two hours
Hang outdoors with heavy clothes pegs clamped to the neckline
Hang by the shoulders from a wire hanger while soaking wet
10.explanation: Wet wool loses tensile resilience; gravitational water weight drags wet vertical garments out of shape unless supported horizontally.

10.question: What is 'moth damage' on wool clothing and what actually eats the wool fibres?
options: Moth wings that rub against the fabric and wear it out
Clothes moth larvae (caterpillars) that hatch from microscopic eggs and feed on keratin protein, chewing small irregular holes in the cloth
Adult flying moths that bite holes in wool with sharp teeth
Chemical poison sprayed by adult moths onto wool sweaters
10.explanation: Adult moths do not feed; newly hatched Tineola bisselliella larvae digest keratin protein, thriving in dark wardrobes on soiled wool fibers.

10.question: How can wool garments be protected from moth infestation during long-term seasonal storage?
options: Spray garments with sweet sugar syrup to deter insects
Store dirty garments in a warm, damp basement corner
Leave garments lying on the floor in an open closet
Wash or dry clean garments before storage (removing sweat/food oils), and store in sealed, airtight bags with cedar wood or lavender
10.explanation: Soiled wool containing perspiration and food stains attracts ovipositing females; airtight bags and volatile botanical oils deter infestation.

10.question: What is the correct way to remove an oily or greasy food stain from a washable cotton shirt?
options: Soak the garment in boiling vinegar for twenty-four hours
Iron the oily stain immediately with an extremely hot iron
Treat promptly: apply a concentrated liquid detergent or dish soap directly to the dry stain, let it penetrate, then wash at the warmest safe temperature
Rub the stain with dry sandpaper until a hole appears
10.explanation: Surfactants emulsify hydrophobic lipid molecules prior to water exposure, whereas hot ironing polymerizes and bakes grease permanently into fibres.

10.question: What is the correct treatment for a fresh, wet blood stain on clothing?
options: Rinse immediately with COLD water (never hot water, which coagulates and bakes protein permanently into the fibres), then wash with enzyme detergent
Cover the stain with dark black ink to hide the red colour
Pour boiling water directly onto the fresh blood stain
Iron the wet blood stain with a hot steam iron immediately
10.explanation: Heat denatures and coagulates hemoglobin protein into insoluble cross-linked complexes; cold water flushes soluble blood albumin out effortlessly.

10.question: What is 'ethical fashion'?
options: Clothing manufactured without using any sewing machines
Garments designed without using any bright or colorful dyes
Fashion that respects human rights, guarantees fair living wages and safe working conditions for garment workers, and opposes child labor
Clothing worn exclusively by legal court judges and lawyers
10.explanation: Ethical fashion addresses supply-chain human rights: eradicating sweatshops, enforcing ILO standards, and ensuring transparency in offshore factories.

10.question: What historic industrial tragedy occurred at the Rana Plaza garment factory in Bangladesh in 2013?
options: A giant fire that destroyed an entire city shopping mall
The catastrophic collapse of an unsafe 8-storey commercial building, killing over 1,130 garment workers and sparking global demands for factory safety reforms
A flood that washed thousands of t-shirts into the ocean
A strike where workers refused to sew buttons on shirts
10.explanation: The disaster highlighted structural safety negligence in fast-fashion outsourcing, leading to the legally binding Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety.

10.question: What is the 'Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh'?
options: A treaty banning the export of clothing from Asian countries
An agreement requiring all garment factories to be painted yellow
A law ordering all clothes to be sewn by hand without machines
A legally binding agreement between global fashion brands and trade unions to mandate independent safety inspections and remediate dangerous factory buildings
10.explanation: Independent structural engineering audits, worker complaint hotlines, and mandatory brand remediation funding transformed factory structural safety.

10.question: What is 'sweatshop labor' in global apparel production?
options: A dry cleaning shop where clothes are pressed with steam
A studio where sportswear is manufactured for athletes
A factory where workers exercise on treadmills while sewing
Workplace environments characterized by dangerously poor working conditions, poverty wages, excessive forced overtime, child labor, and worker abuse
10.explanation: Exploitative subcontracting drives low tier-2/3 factory wages down, enforcing long shifts in unventilated, hazardous facilities lacking labor rights.

10.question: What is a 'living wage' versus a statutory 'minimum wage' for garment workers?
options: A living wage covers the actual basic cost of living (food, clean water, housing, healthcare, education, clothing, and modest savings); minimum wage is often far lower
A living wage is paid in fresh food rather than paper money
A living wage is money given to workers after they retire
A living wage is paid only to workers who live inside the factory
10.explanation: In many garment-exporting nations, legal minimum wages fall 50–70% below basic basket-of-goods living wage benchmarks, perpetuating poverty.

10.question: What is 'fair trade' certification in the cotton and apparel industry?
options: An agreement allowing companies to trade clothes without paying taxes
A system where clothing is given away to customers for free
A competition to find the fastest sewing machine operator
A system guaranteeing smallholder farmers and workers fair floor prices, sustainable production standards, and an additional community social development premium
10.explanation: Fairtrade minimum prices protect cotton growers from volatile commodity market crashes, while social premiums fund village schools and water wells.

10.question: What is 'child labor' in the textile and agriculture supply chain?
options: The employment of children below legal minimum working ages that deprives them of their childhood, education, and harms their physical and mental development
Teaching a child how to sew a button onto their own shirt at home
A teenager working part-time for two hours on a weekend in a shop
Children wearing uniforms to attend primary school classes
10.explanation: ILO Conventions 138 and 182 ban hazardous child exploitation in hazardous cotton harvesting, ginning mills, and informal subcontracted stitching units.

10.question: What is 'supply chain transparency' in the fashion industry?
options: Selling clothes in clear plastic transparent shopping bags
Painting factory windows with clear glass so tourists can watch
Brands publicly disclosing the names, locations, and working conditions of all factories and sub-suppliers involved in manufacturing their garments
Making garments from transparent, clear plastic fabrics
10.explanation: Publishing Tier-1 to Tier-4 supplier lists enables NGOs and consumers to verify human rights compliance, environmental audits, and ethical sourcing.

10.question: What is the 'Fashion Revolution' movement and the '#Whomademyclothes' campaign?
options: A company that sells antique military uniforms to museums
A global activist movement founded after the Rana Plaza disaster that demands transparency, sustainability, and worker rights in the fashion industry
A fashion show where models walk backwards down the runway
A political party that wants to outlaw the wearing of trousers
10.explanation: Annual Fashion Revolution Weeks mobilize social media pressure, demanding corporate accountability and transparent disclosures across supply tiers.

10.question: What is 'deadstock fabric'?
options: A piece of black mourning cloth used at funeral services
Leftover, unsold, or surplus fabric from textile mills and fashion brand cancellations that would otherwise be discarded or incinerated
Fabric that has been buried in garden soil for fifty years
Fabric woven from the wool of dead farm animals
10.explanation: Sourcing surplus mill over-runs rescues pristine luxury textiles from waste incinerators, providing eco-conscious indie designers with circular yardage.

10.question: What is 'circular fashion'?
options: Sewing clothes in circular hoop shapes instead of normal patterns
A fashion store built inside a circular concrete building
Wearing a circular hula-hoop around the waist like a skirt
A regenerative textile system where clothes are designed to be durable, rented, repaired, resold, and recycled, keeping materials out of landfills indefinitely
10.explanation: Replacing linear 'take-make-waste' models with biological closed loops (compostable fibers) and technical loops (PET bottle/polyester depolymerization).

10.question: What is 'garment rental' and 'fashion subscription' services?
options: Donating old clothes to charitable organizations in bins
Paying a monthly fee to borrow sewing machines from a library
Buying second-hand clothes at weekend outdoor flea markets
Business models where consumers rent clothing for temporary use (e.g. weddings, parties, designer wear) rather than buying new items permanently
10.explanation: Product-as-a-service models maximize garment utilization rates, curbing the carbon and resource footprint of single-use formal and occasion wear.

10.question: What is the 'second-hand' (thrift / vintage) clothing market?
options: Wearing clothes that were made five hundred years ago in museums
Buying and selling previously owned and worn clothing, extending garment lifespans and reducing demand for new virgin textile manufacturing
Purchasing clothes made entirely from recycled plastic bottles
Buying brand new clothes that have never been worn before
10.explanation: Extending garment use by just nine months reduces carbon, water, and waste footprints by ~20–30%, powering platforms like Depop and Vinted.

10.question: What is 'visible mending' (such as Japanese Sashiko)?
options: Covering a hole with sticky scotch tape from the inside
Throwing away a jacket as soon as a small tear appears in the elbow
Repairing clothes using invisible transparent nylon threads
A creative textile repair philosophy where tears and holes are repaired using contrasting decorative stitching, celebrating the garment's history and repair
10.explanation: Sashiko running stitches and boro patching reinforce worn denim with geometrical embroidery, embracing wabi-sabi aesthetics and repair culture.

10.question: Why is the production of conventionally grown cotton environmentally intensive?
options: Cotton can only be grown inside expensive heated glasshouses
Cotton manufacturing releases radioactive nuclear waste into rivers
It consumes vast quantities of freshwater for irrigation and requires heavy applications of toxic chemical insecticides and synthetic fertilisers
Cotton requires trees to be cut down across thousands of hectares
10.explanation: Accounting for ~16% of global insecticide use, conventional cotton cultivation depletes local aquifers (e.g. Aral Sea) and causes soil toxicity.

10.question: What ecological disaster was caused primarily by massive irrigation diversions for cotton cultivation in Central Asia?
options: The freezing of Lake Geneva into solid ice in winter
The creation of a giant ocean coral reef in the Sahara desert
The flooding of the Amazon river basin in South America
The near-total drying up and environmental devastation of the Aral Sea
10.explanation: Diverting the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for monoculture cotton irrigation shrunk the Aral Sea by 90%, leaving toxic salinized dust bowls.

10.question: What is 'waterless dyeing' technology (e.g. DryDye / supercritical CO2 dyeing)?
options: Exposing clothes to bright sunlight to fade them into new colours
Dyeing clothes by burying them in dry desert sand for three days
Painting clothes with dry powder chalk using handheld brushes
Using recycled supercritical carbon dioxide under pressure to dissolve and infuse dyes into synthetic fibres without using a single drop of water
10.explanation: Supercritical CO2 acts as a solvent fluid at 120°C and 250 bar, diffusing disperse dyes into polyester and eliminating wastewater effluent completely.

10.question: What is 'cradle-to-cradle' design in the fashion industry?
options: Burying clothes in municipal landfill dumps after five years of wear
Manufacturing clothing designed exclusively for newborn babies in cribs
Designing garments using safe, non-toxic materials that can either completely biodegrade into soil nutrients or be perpetually recycled into new fibres
A design that breaks after being worn for two days in a row
10.explanation: C2C frameworks segregate technical nutrient polymers from biological cellulosic/protein streams, designing products for infinite closed loops.

10.question: What is 'digital fashion' (virtual clothing)?
options: A t-shirt printed with computer keyboard keys on the chest
Clothes woven with tiny electronic wires that play video games
A smartphone carried in the pocket of a business suit
3D computer-rendered virtual clothing designed for online avatars, social media imagery, and gaming, consuming zero physical fabric or water
10.explanation: Virtual styling reduces physical sample waste during B2B design prototyping and satisfies digital self-expression without physical resource throughput.

10.question: How does 3D digital sampling (e.g. CLO 3D, Browzwear) benefit sustainable fashion design?
options: Designers can test fit, drape, and styling on virtual 3D avatars, eliminating multiple rounds of physical sample garments and courier shipping waste
It eliminates the need for human models in retail fashion stores
It sews real physical clothes automatically in five seconds
It turns digital pixels into solid silk fabric bolts
10.explanation: Virtual prototyping cuts physical development samples by 70%, slashing fabric scrap waste, sample yardage production, and international air shipping.

10.question: What is an 'apparel carbon footprint'?
options: The shoe size of the factory manager who operates the sewing line
The amount of charcoal dust used to dye black cotton fabrics
The physical weight of a wool winter coat measured on scales
The total greenhouse gas emissions generated across a garment's life cycle: fibre farming, manufacturing, transport, washing, and final disposal
10.explanation: Assessing Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions highlights that raw material production (~38%) and customer laundering (~20%) dominate apparel emissions.

10.question: What simple consumer laundry habit saves significant household energy and prolongs garment lifespan?
options: Washing clothes in boiling water three times every single day
Ironing wet garments with an iron set to maximum heat
Washing clothes in cold water (30°C or below) and air-drying on a clothesline instead of using high-heat tumble dryers
Using an entire bottle of laundry bleach in every wash load
10.explanation: Cold washing cuts laundry electricity demand by up to 90%, reduces microfibre shedding, prevents thermal shrinkage, and preserves elastane stretch.

10.question: What does 'extending garment active lifespan' accomplish in environmental conservation?
options: It causes clothing factories to go bankrupt and close down permanently
It turns old clothes into radioactive hazardous nuclear waste
Keeping clothes in active use for longer through care, repair, and resale directly offsets the energy, water, and waste burdens of manufacturing new clothing
It forces all people to wear identical uniform clothing every day
10.explanation: WRAP studies confirm that doubling garment active wear life reduces total carbon emissions, water consumption, and municipal waste by over 40%.
